passages.happening:
The book is ‘the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel through Malachi’ (verse 1). God's first word is love. ‘I have loved you,’ says the LORD. But you ask, ‘How have You loved us?’ (verse 2).

God answers by pointing to two brothers. Esau was Jacob's brother, yet God chose Jacob, and he says, ‘but Esau I have hated, and I have made his mountains a wasteland’ (verse 3). Edom, the nation that came from Esau, may say it will rebuild its ruins, but God says, ‘They may build, but I will demolish’ (verse 4). Israel will see it and say, ‘The LORD is great’, even beyond Israel's borders (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers had been home from exile for decades. The temple was rebuilt, but Judah was still a small, poor province of Persia, and the glory the prophets promised had not come. So when God says he has loved them, their reply is honest and tired: how?

Edom lived southeast of the Dead Sea. The two nations had a long, bitter history, and Edom was remembered for joining in when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. In the century that followed, Edom's own land was laid waste, and Arab peoples, later known as the Nabataeans, moved into it. That ruin is the evidence God points to. Judah had been brought home; Edom had not.

The word burden in verse 1 is a prophet's heavy word. It also heads Zechariah 9 and 12.
passages.later: Before the twins were born, God told Rebekah, ‘the older will serve the younger’ (Genesis 25:23). Paul quotes Malachi's line: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Romans 9:13).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that God loved Jacob and hated Esau?

In Malachi the pair speaks first of nations, Israel and Edom, and of God's choice of Jacob's line to carry his covenant. Set side by side in Hebrew, love and hate often mean choosing and not choosing. Jacob ‘loved Rachel more than Leah’, and Genesis then says that Leah was unloved (Genesis 29:30-31). The evidence Malachi gives is history: Edom's land lies in ruins, while Israel has been brought back. It is not a statement of God's feelings toward Esau as a person, and Genesis shows God giving Esau land and descendants (Genesis 33 and 36).

Paul quotes the line to argue that God's promises never depended on descent or effort but on his free choosing. How far that argument reaches is debated, and this site takes no side. Reformed interpreters read Romans 9 as teaching God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation. Many Arminian and other interpreters read it as God's choice of peoples and roles in the story of redemption, noting that Malachi speaks of nations. Both agree that God's choosing is grace, never earned, and that Malachi's point is to assure a doubting people of his love.
passages.asks: The people asked God how he had loved them. Ask what makes you ask that question. And ask what evidence of his faithfulness you might be overlooking.

passages.happening:
‘A son honors his father, and a servant his master. But if I am a father, where is My honor?’ (verse 6). God speaks to the priests who despise his name, and they ask how. By offering defiled food on his altar and calling the table of the LORD contemptible (verse 7). They offer blind, lame and sick animals. “Try offering them to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or show you favor?” (verse 8).

God wishes someone would shut the temple doors, so that the useless fires on his altar would stop. ‘I take no pleasure in you’ (verse 10). ‘For My name will be great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets’ (verse 11). But the priests say of the altar, “Oh, what a nuisance!” and turn up their noses at it (verse 13). Cursed is the cheat who vows a good male animal and sacrifices a damaged one, ‘For I am a great King,’ says the LORD of Hosts (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The law required that animals offered to God be without defect. A sacrifice was a gift from the worshiper's own flock, and a blemished animal said that God deserved the leftovers. The table of the LORD is the altar. Parts of many offerings also fed the priests, which makes their complaint about the food all the more telling.

The governor was the Persian-era official who ruled Judah for the king. No priest would dare give him a sick animal as a gift, yet they gave one to God.

A vow was a promise to give God a particular animal in return for his help. Substituting a worse one afterward was fraud. God keeps speaking of his own name, and that repetition carries the chapter: the priests who should guard it despise it, while the nations will make it great.
passages.later: The law was plain: ‘You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be accepted on your behalf’ (Leviticus 22:20). It forbade offering animals that were lame or blind (Deuteronomy 15:21).
passages.asks: The priests would never give their governor what they gave God. Ask where you give God the leftovers of your time, attention or money. And ask what helps worship stop feeling like a nuisance.
